title: When One Step Is Enough: An Empirical Study of Euler Integration in Flow-Matching Policies

paper.title: When One Step Is Enough: An Empirical Study of Euler Integration in Flow-Matching Policies
paper.abstract:
Abstract Flow matching is now the dominant approach for vision-language action (VLA) robot policies, thanks to its expressiveness and simple training objective.
However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment.
While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary.
We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity.
Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: 1-step vs. reference-step success rates (SR) across all (model, benchmark) cells in our study; Δ = SR ref − SR 1 \Delta=\text{SR}_{\text{ref}}-\text{SR}_{1} is the performance gap in percentage points (pp). Points on or near the x=y diagonal indicate a negligible performance gap between the two conditions. For the three larger models ( π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , LAP, XR-0) all reported gaps are small and either statistically equivalent under two one-sided t-tests (TOST) or inconclusive with one-step having a higher aggregate SR. In the real world pooled deltas Δ \Delta are at most 3.7 3.7\, pp, although with some task-level differences. Diffusion and flow matching models have now become the common choice for training robotic control policies for manipulation [ 8 , 35 , 41 , 26 , 13 ] , consistently outperforming simple regression/Gaussian baselines. To generate action samples, these models learn a vector field that drives noise samples, taken from a source distribution, to a target distribution. Of these, flow matching is now the dominant paradigm by virtue of its simpler form (solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE) instead of a stochastic differential equation (SDE)). Many of the latest robot foundation models, in the form of vision-language-action (VLA) models, combine a large, pretrained vision-language model (VLM) backbone [ 21 , 37 , 3 , 1 ] , providing existing image and text understanding, with a flow matching action head [ 32 , 43 , 29 , 4 , 39 , 5 ] . In flow matching policies, a velocity field is learned and generating actions requires integrating the learned velocity field, typically with an Euler integrator that evaluates the network N N times. Higher N N results in lower discretization error at the cost of increased latency, thus limiting control frequency, and subsequently hurting fluid motion in dynamic or contact-rich tasks. Recent works mitigate these issues by distilling the multi-step policy into a single-step proxy [ 26 ] , introducing distribution-shaping objectives that are expensive for large-scale VLAs [ 16 ] , or augmenting the flow matching objective to encourage straight-line flows that need fewer integration steps [ 27 , 38 , 11 , 12 ] . This multi-step formulation also necessitates backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) for gradient-based optimization of reinforcement learning (RL) objectives, which is costly and prone to unstable gradients. Due to the simplicity of its formulation, in practice VLAs are trained with the rectified flow matching objective) [ 19 ] , where the target velocity along each training pair is constant, producing linear interpolation paths between source and target samples. It is not the case in general that the learned trajectories are straight, as intersecting linear paths produce curved learned trajectories, which in image generation degrades single-step sample quality [ 19 ] . However, for robot control, given the current observation and state, the nature of the conditional target distribution may differ substantially from the image generation setting. Prior work [ 25 ] finds that, for control policies, the performance advantage of generative models over regression ones mainly comes from stochasticity injection and the dense supervision signal during training, rather than from modeling multimodality, which they find largely absent in robotics datasets (including the ones understood to be multimodal like Push T ), likely due to their high-dimensional observation space. Concurrent work [ 7 ] reaches a similar conclusion for VLAs, but studies a single architecture, focusing on training hyperparameters on LIBERO [ 18 ] and its variants, with a small real-world experiment. In contrast, we study six VLAs across multiple benchmarks, run a large-scale real-world evaluation, and analyse the smoothness and diversity of the generated trajectories. We ask whether large-scale VLAs trained with the rectified flow objective and no additional regularization can be integrated in a single step at inference without loss of performance. We answer this question with what is, to our knowledge, the first paired one-step vs multi-step ablation of flow matching VLAs, covering six VLAs across multiple benchmarks. We evaluate six flow matching VLA models spanning 450 450 M to 4.7 4.7 B parameters (SmolVLA [ 32 ] , FLOWER [ 29 ] , X-VLA [ 43 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 4 ] , LAP [ 39 ] , XR-0 [ 5 ] ) on four simulation benchmarks (LIBERO [ 18 ] , LIBERO+ [ 10 ] , CALVIN [ 23 ] , RoboTwin 2.0 [ 6 ] ) and a real world Franka suite [ 42 ] . All comparisons use matched seeds and real world paired testing. We compare success rates through the two one-sided t-tests (TOST) equivalence test [ 30 ] , analyse the difference in smoothness and diversity of the generated trajectories and also report a latency comparison. Results are summarised in Fig. 1 . Our findings are as follows: • Step-equivalence is a factor of model scale, VLM pretraining and training maturity: The four largest VLAs show strong robustness to single-step inference across simulation benchmarks. π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and XR-0 are statistically equivalent within 3 3 percentage points (pp) on every simulation benchmark for which a public checkpoint was available. X-VLA and LAP are equivalent on all but one benchmark each (Sec. 4.1 ). Initialization ablations further suggest that pretrained visual-language representations favour step-equivalence, even without robot-action pretraining, and the difference between one-step and multi-step inference fades with longer fine-tuning (Sec. 4.5 ). Similarly, for the real world, multi-step inference confers no consistent advantage in terms of success rate or trajectory smoothness (Sec. 4.1 and 4.3 ). • Longer task horizons expose greater sensitivity to inference steps: The two smaller models (FLOWER, SmolVLA) retain a performance gap that is larger on long-horizon tasks while their short-horizon performance is more robust to the number of integration steps (Sec. 4.1 ). Importantly, additional Euler steps do not always help: the direction of the performance gap varies across the smaller models (Sec. 4.1 and 4.5 ). • Practical payoff: For most current flow matching VLAs, multi-step inference does not improve performance over one step, enabling 1.6 1.6 - 4.8 × 4.8\times lower latency at deployment (Sec. 4.2 ). Taken together, these results reframe the conventional wisdom around inference in VLAs. While a growing body of work proposes auxiliary objectives explicitly to recover the single-step regime, we find that for the dominant class of present day flow matching VLAs, the single-step regime is already accessible without any retraining, architectural changes, or additional regularization.

sections.heading: 2.1 Flow matching models
sections.text: Flow matching [ 17 ] is a generative modelling framework that learns a time-dependent velocity field v θ ​ ( x t , t ) v_{\theta}(x_{t},t) defining a continuous-time transport from a source distribution p 0 p_{0} to a target data distribution p 1 p_{1} . The transport is described by the ordinary differential equation (ODE) d ​ x t d ​ t = v θ ​ ( x t , t ) , x 0 ∼ p 0 , t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \frac{dx_{t}}{dt}=v_{\theta}(x_{t},t),\qquad x_{0}\sim p_{0},t\in[0,1] (1) that converts x 0 ∼ p 0 x_{0}\sim p_{0} to x 1 ∼ p 1 x_{1}\sim p_{1} . In rectified flow matching [ 19 ] , the driving velocity field is set to follow the direction of the linear path from x 0 x_{0} to x 1 x_{1} , i.e., v θ ​ ( x t , t ) = x 1 − x 0 {v_{\theta}(x_{t},t)=x_{1}-x_{0}} , resulting in x t = ( 1 − t ) ​ x 0 + t ​ x 1 {x_{t}=(1-t)\,x_{0}+t\,x_{1}} . The reference N N reported by published VLAs ranges from 4 4 to 10 10 (Tab. 1 ). In this work, we ask whether using N = 1 N=1 leads to a drop in performance for robot action generation.

sections.heading: 2.2 Accelerating flow and diffusion inference
sections.text: The cost of iterative sampling has motivated a broad line of work on reducing the number of integration steps required at inference time. Consistency models [ 14 ] , shortcut models [ 11 ] , and MeanFlow [ 12 ] augment the training objective to recover the multi-step solution from a single forward pass. The motivation for doing so is well-documented in image generation, where the quality of the generated image shows that vanilla flow and diffusion models degrade sharply when collapsed into a few Euler steps [ 31 ] , which further motivates work on improved ODE solvers and sampling schedules [ 34 , 20 ] . The few-step methods that have been applied to robotics, MeanFlow [ 40 ] and ManiFlow [ 38 ] , were evaluated on small-scale policies where empirically vanilla flow matching policies with single-step inference perform substantially worse than with multi-step inference. Recent work [ 25 ] shows that the choice of the model architecture is a major component of policy performance. This motivates asking whether the one-step degradation actually remains with large flow matching VLAs and, to the best of our knowledge, this has not been thoroughly investigated.

sections.heading: 3 Experimental Design
sections.text: Our central question is whether the multi-step Euler integration is buying meaningful improvements in task success rates over a single Euler step. We answer this with a paired comparison protocol. For each (model, benchmark) pair, we take a single trained policy, and evaluate once with the reference number of integration steps reported by the original paper, and once with a single Euler step. To reduce stochasticity in the evaluation process, for every (model, benchmark) pair, the 1-step and reference-step rollouts have the same initial conditions [ 2 ] . In simulation this means matched initial seeds for each episode trial. For real world evaluation, trials are run as paired A/B tests. To further control for experimenter bias, the experimenter is blind to the variant being tested. Finally, in real world experiments we also seed the noise sampled from the policy before every rollout within the pair.

sections.heading: 3.2 Benchmarks
sections.text: We evaluate seven models across four simulation benchmarks and one real world suite. Simulation Benchmarks: We test all the models on the LIBERO [ 18 ] benchmark. LIBERO has four task suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, LIBERO-10), each comprising 10 tasks. We report aggregate results over the Spatial, Object and Goal suites (denoted as SGO), and separate results for the long-horizon LIBERO-10 suite. For evaluation, we run 50 50 trials per task, totalling 2000 2000 trials per model variant. To test our hypothesis against distribution shift, we also test the models on LIBERO+ [ 10 ] , a perturbation-extended version of LIBERO with 10 030 10\,030 task instances. We also evaluate on the CALVIN ABC → \rightarrow D [ 23 ] setting that tests for zero shot generalization. CALVIN is a long-horizon language-conditioned benchmark, and evaluation requires policies to complete a sequence of 5 tasks across 1000 1000 instruction chains. We report SR@5 (full-chain success) and average chain length. Finally, we also include the RoboTwin 2.0 [ 6 ] benchmark, a 50 50 -task bimanual manipulation benchmark with two difficulty regimes (”clean” and ”randomised”). We use the matched-seed paired protocol ( 100 100 episodes per task) from the original benchmark, yielding 5000 5000 paired episodes per regime per (model, number of steps) cell. Separately, we also examine how the different models behave on one task from D3IL [ 9 ] , a benchmark that explicitly evaluates the model’s ability to learn multimodal behaviours. Real world Franka suite: This consists of four in-house kitchen-style tasks using a Franka Emika Panda arm (Fig. 2 ): spoon to drawer (longest-horizon, pick-and-place), open drawer (contact-rich), open oven (precise manipulation), and close oven (short horizon task). The training dataset is the same as the one used in [ 42 ] . We run 100 100 trials per task per (model, num steps), totalling 400 400 episodes per model variant and a total of 4800 4800 rollouts. Additional evaluation details are provided in the Appendix (Table D4 ). Figure 2: Real world Franka suite: spoon drawer , open drawer , open oven , close oven (left to right).

sections.heading: 3.3 Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: To claim a positive equivalence we test our hypothesis of step-invariance through the TOST procedure [ 30 ] (see Tab. 2 ). We conduct this test aggregating results across tasks within a benchmark: this violates the i.i.d. assumption for the samples of the compared distributions, but the effect is negligible and recommended practice in prior work [ 2 ] . For real world experiments, due to a more restricted evaluation budget than simulation, we report and discuss the confidence intervals (CIs) of the difference between the approaches, and conduct a McNemar analysis (see Tab. 3 and Sec. B.2 ). We also investigate the quality of the executed real world trajectories through a jerk analysis (see Fig. 3 ). For a per-task breakdown we refer to Sec. E . For TOST, we set a margin of practical equivalence of δ = 3 ​ pp \delta=3\,\textrm{pp} (percentage points) when comparing success rates, and δ = 0.15 \delta=0.15 when comparing chain length for CALVIN 1 1 1 The chain length in CALVIN is up to 5, so we map 3 3\, pp to this range and a confidence level α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 . To claim equivalence, TOST needs to reject two composite null hypotheses, hence the CIs will be computed at a confidence of 90 % 90\% , i.e., 100 ​ ( 1 − 2 ​ α ) % 100(1-2\alpha)\% . We declare the two methods equivalent within the margin δ \delta iff the CI for the difference in means of the two distributions is strictly contained in [ − δ , δ ] [-\delta,\delta] , we declare a relevant difference if it lies completely outside of it, and otherwise the test is inconclusive (more details in Sec. B ).

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Results
sections.text: We evaluate every (model, benchmark) cell and report results in Tables 2 and 3 : among the 36 test cells in simulation benchmarks 23 show equivalence, 4 show that multi-step is better, 2 show that 1-step is better, and 7 are inconclusive. Step-equivalence appears in models trained on different pretraining corpora, in different codebases, and under different architectural and hyperparameter choices. The presence of this phenomenon across heterogeneous pipelines suggests that it is an effect of well-trained rectified-flow VLAs rather than an artifact of any single model, codebase, or benchmark. The remaining performance gaps are concentrated 1) on long horizon suites, and 2) mainly among ≤ 1 \leq 1 B models (DiT, SmolVLA, FLOWER). On short horizon suites and for every model ≥ 1 \geq 1 B, single and multi-step inference performance are equivalent based on our tests. A trajectory-smoothness analysis in the real world (Sec. 4.3 ) points the same way: multi-step yields smoother motion only for the two sub-1B models, while for every larger model one-step is marginally smoother. Finally, in Sec. 4.4 , we find that, while not reducing the success rate, one-step inference yields less diverse trajectories.

sections.heading: 4.2 Inference Latency
sections.text: On a single A100 GPU, collapsing to 1-step cuts latency by 1.6 × 1.6\times to 4.8 × 4.8\times , raising the achievable control frequency (see Tab. 1 ). Since only the action head re-runs per Euler step, models with a small action head relative to the VLM gain the least ( π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , 1.6 × 1.6\times ), while those where the action head is comparable gain the most (SmolVLA, 4.8 × 4.8\times ). For the larger models, the latency gains generally come at little cost to task success, with the exceptions noted above.

sections.heading: 4.3 Trajectory smoothness
sections.text: Figure 3: Paired jerk-RMS comparison of real world rollouts. Violins are kernel density estimates; boxes give quartiles with 5–95% whiskers; the coloured line is the median. n n is the number of samples (pairs with both runs successful). Beyond success rates, we ask whether one-step inference changes the smoothness of the executed motion. To quantify trajectory smoothness we use the per-episode root mean square (RMS) of the joint jerk: after recording the executed joint trajectory, we first smooth it with a Savitzky-Golay filter (polynomial of order 3 3 , window size 11 11 ) and then compute the jerk via finite differences. Because failure modes can produce different jerk profiles, we only compare episodes where both approaches succeed. We report the per-model distribution of the log ratio of the paired joint-space jerk in Fig. 3 . We find no consistent smoothness cost to one-step inference: the multi step reference is meaningfully smoother only for two sub-1B models (DiT, FLOWER), while for every model above 1B, one-step is in fact marginally smoother, echoing the scale-dependence of our task-success results.

sections.heading: 4.4 Trajectory diversity
sections.text: (a) Success rate with 95% CIs and normalised entropy (b) Trajectories executed by π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} Figure 4: D3IL Avoiding results. In (a), ∗ indicates a significant McNemar difference ( p < 0.05 {p<0.05} ). We evaluated the models on D3IL Avoiding [ 9 ] , a multimodal control task with 24 valid success modes, to study policy behaviour diversity. As the original benchmark only has a state-based version of the Avoiding task, we built a visual version of this dataset by collecting image data replaying the state demos. We evaluated each model through 200 evaluation episodes on matched initial state and policy noise stream. Fine-tuning details can be found in Tab. D2 and Sec. D.2 . As shown in Fig. 4(a) , one-step inference improves performance for DiT and FLOWER, degrades it for X-VLA, while among larger models one-step inference consistently does not hurt success rate, even increasing it for LAP and XR-0. However, it changes behaviour diversity by generating trajectories with less entropy, i.e., concentrating the generated trajectories on fewer valid strategies. Under one-step inference, DiT, FLOWER, and LAP each produce a single successful strategy, yielding zero strategy entropy, whilst maintaining success rates of at least 99.5%. Multi-step inference recovers multiple successful strategies, although with lower overall success. For the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} model, while the two approaches have similar success rates, one-step inference has far less entropy, and the number of observed successful strategies drops from 19 to 8 (Fig. 4(b) ). Together, these findings suggest that one-step inference does not hurt success rate, but does narrow the range of generated behaviours.

sections.heading: 4.5 Ablations
sections.text: Figure 5: Step-count gap over training on LIBERO. Each panel reports Δ = SR ref − SR 1 \Delta=\text{SR}_{\text{ref}}-\text{SR}_{1} with shaded area as 90% CIs. Multi-step gains, when present, are concentrated on LIBERO-10 and fade with training. The short-horizon suites are close to step-invariant throughout. The main results show that multi-step Euler inference does not guarantee higher success rates for current flow matching VLAs. We now investigate two questions: (Q1) How do model scale and pretraining influence step-equivalence? (Q2) How does the gap evolve over the course of training? We focus on LIBERO because it contains both short-horizon SGO suites, and the longer-horizon LIBERO-10 suite, where most of the performance gaps appear. Our findings are visualised in Fig. 5 . Q1: How do model scale and pretraining influence step-equivalence? We first consider the randomly initialised π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} (scratch; Fig. 5 , third column). It favours one-step inference throughout training and has not reached step-equivalence by the final checkpoint, although its gap narrows substantially (from − 20 -20 to − 3 -3 pp on SGO with a [ − 4.38 , − 1.64 ] [-4.38,-1.64] CI). In the second column of Fig. 5 , we omit the from-scratch X-VLA variant because of its low absolute task performance: across evaluated checkpoints and inference-step settings, success rates remain below 10% on LIBERO-10, 5% on Goal, and 20% on Spatial, and peak at 42.8% on Object. Despite its low absolute performance, from-scratch X-VLA favours one-step inference more often, including on pooled SGO at the final two checkpoints, where the 90% CIs for the performance gap lie entirely below zero. Thus, within our training budget, step-equivalence does not emerge from random initialization, though the converging trend for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} suggests that longer training might close the gap. To identify which kind of pretraining matters, we compare different initializations for both π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and X-VLA: a generic VLM (PaliGemma2 [ 3 ] or Florence [ 37 ] , respectively) with a randomly initialised action expert, the VLA’s own VLM backbone (trained also on robot data) with a randomly initialised action expert, and the fully pretrained VLA. For both models, all three achieve step-equivalence on SGO and reach near-zero gaps by the final checkpoint, so robot-action pretraining is not required. However, pretrained vision-language features alone are not sufficient: the 211M DiT, which conditions on pretrained CLIP image and text encoders [ 28 ] but trains the remaining model from scratch, develops a multi-step advantage on LIBERO-10 that grows to 15 15\, pp over training (first column), echoing our scale-dependent main results. Q2: How does the gap evolve over the course of training? π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} is step-equivalent on SGO from the earliest checkpoint. For X-VLA, early in training, additional Euler steps hurt performance, and this gap collapses by the final checkpoint. FLOWER is the clearest case where multi-step helps, but the benefit is localised to LIBERO-10 at early and intermediate checkpoints, while the short-horizon SGO gap remains near zero and step-equivalence is verified on both SGO and LIBERO-10 at the last checkpoint (Fig. 5 , rightmost column). This last point resolves an apparent tension with Tab. 2 where FLOWER shows a residual gap on LIBERO while X-VLA, a model of similar scale ( 950 950 M), does not. The discrepancy is one of checkpoint selection, not scale. The authors of FLOWER train their model for up to 40 epochs but mention that they use early stopping and for LIBERO use the checkpoint at epoch 19. Our ablation sweep instead retains all checkpoints during training, and at the final checkpoint FLOWER’s step-count performance gap disappears, bringing it in line with X-VLA. The Tab. 2 gap therefore reflects an early-stopped checkpoint evaluated before step-invariance has fully emerged, rather than a property of FLOWER’s scale or architecture. Together, these refine the main claim: step-equivalence is favoured by larger models, generic VLM pretraining, and longer fine-tuning. When one of these properties is missing, tasks with longer horizons tend to show step-dependence.

sections.heading: 5 Limitations
sections.text: To aid reproducibility and avoid confounding step-invariance with our own training decisions, we deliberately used released checkpoints as-is rather than fine-tuning base models for all our evaluations in simulation. The downside is uneven coverage: not every model ships a checkpoint for every benchmark, so some (model, benchmark) cells could not be evaluated. A full grid would require training each model on each benchmark, which we leave to future work. While the aggregate results for the real world tasks are close, we observed up to 13 13 pp difference between single- and multi-step regimes on single tasks. Real world evaluation could therefore benefit from an increased dataset size, matching the scale of the simulated benchmarks. Finally, we show the single-step policy matches the multi-step reference in most cases and that single-step gradient computations are therefore cheap. However, we do not run RL experiments to validate that resulting policy gradient updates are stable and effective at VLA scale.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Across six flow matching VLAs from 450M to 4.7B parameters, plus a 211 211\, M DiT, four simulation benchmarks and a real world Franka suite, we find the assumption that multi-step inference is necessary for task performance does not hold for well-trained large VLAs. Where multi-step helps, the benefit is localised to smaller models on long-horizon tasks. Our ablations trace step-invariance to a combination of large scale models, training maturity and the quality of the pretrained VLM features rather than to large-scale robot-action pretraining which we find to be not necessary. The key implication is deployment latency: N N multiplies action-head compute at every replanning step, limiting control frequency. A single Euler step removes this overhead with negligible impact on success rate, enabling low-latency deployment of existing flow-matching VLA checkpoints without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives. The same property makes single-backward-pass actor updates attractive for RL post-training without differentiating through the integration chain. Converting this into a concrete recipe is a promising direction for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Action space disagreement and flow geometry
sections.text: Our main results show that one-step and multi-step Euler inference often achieve statistically equivalent success rates. However, as shown in Sec. 4.4 , similar task performance does not necessarily imply that the two methods produce identical actions. We investigate this distinction by examining how action-space disagreement relates to task success during training in Sec. A.1 , and whether the geometry of the learned flow explains the benefits of additional integration steps A.2 .

sections.heading: A.1 Action space divergence analysis
sections.text: Figure A1: Comparison between the 1-step and 10-step integration approaches: L2 distance in the action space against the absolute value of the success rate gap. Each marker is a checkpoint (labeled 5k–29k), and color/shape of the marker identify the initialization variant. Dashed lines capture per-variant trend. In our ablations (Sec. 4.5 ) we investigated how the success rate (SR) gap between the 1-step and multi-step approach varies during training. To further investigate the mechanism behind this gap, we here analyse the action divergence, i.e., the L2 distance between the 1-step and reference-step actions, which corresponds to 10 steps for the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} model family. We chose to conduct this analysis on the LIBERO benchmark because it contains both short-horizon Spatial, Goal, Object (SGO) suites, and the longer-horizon LIBERO-10 suite. We consider the same four initializations as in Sec. 4.5 : 1) the base 𝝅 0.5 \bm{\pi_{0.5}} model, 2) 𝝅 0.5 \bm{\pi_{0.5}} VLM weights with a randomly initialised action expert, 3) Paligemma VLM initialised with Paligemma2 weights [ 3 ] , and 4) Scratch , where all weights are randomly initialised. All the models are finetuned for 30 000 30\,000 gradient steps and with a batch size of 256. We randomly sample 5,000 5,000 transitions for each LIBERO suite, and measure the L2 distance between actions generated with 1 and 10 Euler steps, using the same initial noise 2 2 2 We report the L2 distance over only the first 3 action dimensions so that the distance has interpretable units ( mm \text{\,}\mathrm{mm} /step). Note that an equivalent plot considering the rotation dimensions ( deg \text{\,}\deg /step) shows the same trend. against the SR gap. Fig. A1 shows that the two quantities shrink together over training as every variant moves toward the origin, but the correlation between the observed gap and the action divergence decreases as the amount of pretraining increases. The pretrained variants 𝝅 0.5 \bm{\pi_{0.5}} VLM and Paligemma VLM can have large action divergence early in training yet exhibit an SR gap of less than five percentage points, while the Scratch variant turns a slightly lower L2 distance into an 18 18 percentage point gap. Thus, the magnitude of action disagreement alone does not determine its effect on task success. We hypothesise that this decoupling reflects multi-modality in the action distribution: with informative VLM features, the 1-step and 10-step solutions can land on different but equally valid action modes, so a large L2 difference need not imply a worse outcome. Without such features, as in the randomly initialised variant, the 1-step approach instead drifts toward genuinely worse actions.

sections.heading: D.1 Real world experiment details
sections.text: Dataset : Our in-house dataset is composed of 68 872 68\,872 frames spanning 410 410 episodes and 9 9 tasks, collected at a frequency of 12.5 Hz 12.5\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} by a single human operator. Tab. D1 lists the prompt and duration associated with each task. Every task is a tabletop task, and together they cover a range of contact-rich interactions: opening and closing hinge joints (the oven) and slide joints (the drawer), precision manipulation in the Open oven task, as well as simpler pick-and-place tasks. The dataset is deliberately designed to require language grounding, i.e., given the same initial state multiple tasks can be carried out depending on the input prompt. Although the dataset consists of 9 tasks, in this work we evaluate only on a subset of 4 tasks. The training dataset is the same as the one used in [ 42 ] . The proprioceptive state of the robot is ( 𝒙 , 𝒓 , g ) \left(\bm{x},\bm{r},g\right) , where 𝒙 ∈ ℝ 3 \bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} is the end effector position, 𝒓 ∈ ℝ 3 \bm{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} is the end effector orientation in axis-angle representation, and g ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] g\in\left[0,1\right] is the gripper state. However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment. While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary. We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity. Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives. Diffusion and flow matching models have now become the common choice for training robotic control policies for manipulation [ 8 , 35 , 41 , 26 , 13 ] , consistently outperforming simple regression/Gaussian baselines. To generate action samples, these models learn a vector field that drives noise samples, taken from a source distribution, to a target distribution. Of these, flow matching is now the dominant paradigm by virtue of its simpler form (solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE) instead of a stochastic differential equation (SDE)). Many of the latest robot foundation models, in the form of vision-language-action (VLA) models, combine a large, pretrained vision-language model (VLM) backbone [ 21 , 37 , 3 , 1 ] , providing existing image and text understanding, with a flow matching action head [ 32 , 43 , 29 , 4 , 39 , 5 ] . In flow matching policies, a velocity field is learned and generating actions requires integrating the learned velocity field, typically with an Euler integrator that evaluates the network N N times. Higher N N results in lower discretization error at the cost of increased latency, thus limiting control frequency, and subsequently hurting fluid motion in dynamic or contact-rich tasks. Recent works mitigate these issues by distilling the multi-step policy into a single-step proxy [ 26 ] , introducing distribution-shaping objectives that are expensive for large-scale VLAs [ 16 ] , or augmenting the flow matching objective to encourage straight-line flows that need fewer integration steps [ 27 , 38 , 11 , 12 ] . This multi-step formulation also necessitates backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) for gradient-based optimization of reinforcement learning (RL) objectives, which is costly and prone to unstable gradients. Due to the simplicity of its formulation, in practice VLAs are trained with the rectified flow matching objective) [ 19 ] , where the target velocity along each training pair is constant, producing linear interpolation paths between source and target samples. It is not the case in general that the learned trajectories are straight, as intersecting linear paths produce curved learned trajectories, which in image generation degrades single-step sample quality [ 19 ] . However, for robot control, given the current observation and state, the nature of the conditional target distribution may differ substantially from the image generation setting. Prior work [ 25 ] finds that, for control policies, the performance advantage of generative models over regression ones mainly comes from stochasticity injection and the dense supervision signal during training, rather than from modeling multimodality, which they find largely absent in robotics datasets (including the ones understood to be multimodal like Push T ), likely due to their high-dimensional observation space. Concurrent work [ 7 ] reaches a similar conclusion for VLAs, but studies a single architecture, focusing on training hyperparameters on LIBERO [ 18 ] and its variants, with a small real-world experiment. In contrast, we study six VLAs across multiple benchmarks, run a large-scale real-world evaluation, and analyse the smoothness and diversity of the generated trajectories. We ask whether large-scale VLAs trained with the rectified flow objective and no additional regularization can be integrated in a single step at inference without loss of performance. We answer this question with what is, to our knowledge, the first paired one-step vs multi-step ablation of flow matching VLAs, covering six VLAs across multiple benchmarks. We evaluate six flow matching VLA models spanning 450 450 M to 4.7 4.7 B parameters (SmolVLA [ 32 ] , FLOWER [ 29 ] , X-VLA [ 43 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 4 ] , LAP [ 39 ] , XR-0 [ 5 ] ) on four simulation benchmarks (LIBERO [ 18 ] , LIBERO+ [ 10 ] , CALVIN [ 23 ] , RoboTwin 2.0 [ 6 ] ) and a real world Franka suite [ 42 ] . All comparisons use matched seeds and real world paired testing. We compare success rates through the two one-sided t-tests (TOST) equivalence test [ 30 ] , analyse the difference in smoothness and diversity of the generated trajectories and also report a latency comparison. Results are summarised in Fig. 1 . Our findings are as follows: • Step-equivalence is a factor of model scale, VLM pretraining and training maturity: The four largest VLAs show strong robustness to single-step inference across simulation benchmarks. π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and XR-0 are statistically equivalent within 3 3 percentage points (pp) on every simulation benchmark for which a public checkpoint was available. X-VLA and LAP are equivalent on all but one benchmark each (Sec. 4.1 ). Initialization ablations further suggest that pretrained visual-language representations favour step-equivalence, even without robot-action pretraining, and the difference between one-step and multi-step inference fades with longer fine-tuning (Sec. 4.5 ). Similarly, for the real world, multi-step inference confers no consistent advantage in terms of success rate or trajectory smoothness (Sec. 4.1 and 4.3 ). • Longer task horizons expose greater sensitivity to inference steps: The two smaller models (FLOWER, SmolVLA) retain a performance gap that is larger on long-horizon tasks while their short-horizon performance is more robust to the number of integration steps (Sec. 4.1 ). Importantly, additional Euler steps do not always help: the direction of the performance gap varies across the smaller models (Sec. 4.1 and 4.5 ). • Practical payoff: For most current flow matching VLAs, multi-step inference does not improve performance over one step, enabling 1.6 1.6 - 4.8 × 4.8\times lower latency at deployment (Sec. 4.2 ). Taken together, these results reframe the conventional wisdom around inference in VLAs. While a growing body of work proposes auxiliary objectives explicitly to recover the single-step regime, we find that for the dominant class of present day flow matching VLAs, the single-step regime is already accessible without any retraining, architectural changes, or additional regularization. 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 Flow matching models Flow matching [ 17 ] is a generative modelling framework that learns a time-dependent velocity field v θ ​ ( x t , t ) v_{\theta}(x_{t},t) defining a continuous-time transport from a source distribution p 0 p_{0} to a target data distribution p 1 p_{1} . Consistency models [ 14 ] , shortcut models [ 11 ] , and MeanFlow [ 12 ] augment the training objective to recover the multi-step solution from a single forward pass. The motivation for doing so is well-documented in image generation, where the quality of the generated image shows that vanilla flow and diffusion models degrade sharply when collapsed into a few Euler steps [ 31 ] , which further motivates work on improved ODE solvers and sampling schedules [ 34 , 20 ] . The few-step methods that have been applied to robotics, MeanFlow [ 40 ] and ManiFlow [ 38 ] , were evaluated on small-scale policies where empirically vanilla flow matching policies with single-step inference perform substantially worse than with multi-step inference. Recent work [ 25 ] shows that the choice of the model architecture is a major component of policy performance. This motivates asking whether the one-step degradation actually remains with large flow matching VLAs and, to the best of our knowledge, this has not been thoroughly investigated. 3 Experimental Design Our central question is whether the multi-step Euler integration is buying meaningful improvements in task success rates over a single Euler step. We answer this with a paired comparison protocol. For each (model, benchmark) pair, we take a single trained policy, and evaluate once with the reference number of integration steps reported by the original paper, and once with a single Euler step. To reduce stochasticity in the evaluation process, for every (model, benchmark) pair, the 1-step and reference-step rollouts have the same initial conditions [ 2 ] . In simulation this means matched initial seeds for each episode trial. For real world evaluation, trials are run as paired A/B tests. To further control for experimenter bias, the experimenter is blind to the variant being tested. Finally, in real world experiments we also seed the noise sampled from the policy before every rollout within the pair. 3.1 Models We evaluate six flow matching VLAs, spanning roughly an order of magnitude in parameter count, and a DiT [ 13 ] baseline trained from scratch on each benchmark (Tab. 1 ). Despite its low absolute performance, from-scratch X-VLA favours one-step inference more often, including on pooled SGO at the final two checkpoints, where the 90% CIs for the performance gap lie entirely below zero. Thus, within our training budget, step-equivalence does not emerge from random initialization, though the converging trend for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} suggests that longer training might close the gap. To identify which kind of pretraining matters, we compare different initializations for both π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and X-VLA: a generic VLM (PaliGemma2 [ 3 ] or Florence [ 37 ] , respectively) with a randomly initialised action expert, the VLA’s own VLM backbone (trained also on robot data) with a randomly initialised action expert, and the fully pretrained VLA. For both models, all three achieve step-equivalence on SGO and reach near-zero gaps by the final checkpoint, so robot-action pretraining is not required. However, pretrained vision-language features alone are not sufficient: the 211M DiT, which conditions on pretrained CLIP image and text encoders [ 28 ] but trains the remaining model from scratch, develops a multi-step advantage on LIBERO-10 that grows to 15 15\, pp over training (first column), echoing our scale-dependent main results. Q2: How does the gap evolve over the course of training? π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} is step-equivalent on SGO from the earliest checkpoint. For X-VLA, early in training, additional Euler steps hurt performance, and this gap collapses by the final checkpoint. FLOWER is the clearest case where multi-step helps, but the benefit is localised to LIBERO-10 at early and intermediate checkpoints, while the short-horizon SGO gap remains near zero and step-equivalence is verified on both SGO and LIBERO-10 at the last checkpoint (Fig. 5 , rightmost column). This last point resolves an apparent tension with Tab. 2 where FLOWER shows a residual gap on LIBERO while X-VLA, a model of similar scale ( 950 950 M), does not. The discrepancy is one of checkpoint selection, not scale. The authors of FLOWER train their model for up to 40 epochs but mention that they use early stopping and for LIBERO use the checkpoint at epoch 19. Our ablation sweep instead retains all checkpoints during training, and at the final checkpoint FLOWER’s step-count performance gap disappears, bringing it in line with X-VLA. The Tab. 2 gap therefore reflects an early-stopped checkpoint evaluated before step-invariance has fully emerged, rather than a property of FLOWER’s scale or architecture. Together, these refine the main claim: step-equivalence is favoured by larger models, generic VLM pretraining, and longer fine-tuning. When one of these properties is missing, tasks with longer horizons tend to show step-dependence. 5 Limitations To aid reproducibility and avoid confounding step-invariance with our own training decisions, we deliberately used released checkpoints as-is rather than fine-tuning base models for all our evaluations in simulation. The downside is uneven coverage: not every model ships a checkpoint for every benchmark, so some (model, benchmark) cells could not be evaluated. A full grid would require training each model on each benchmark, which we leave to future work. While the aggregate results for the real world tasks are close, we observed up to 13 13 pp difference between single- and multi-step regimes on single tasks. Real world evaluation could therefore benefit from an increased dataset size, matching the scale of the simulated benchmarks. Finally, we show the single-step policy matches the multi-step reference in most cases and that single-step gradient computations are therefore cheap. However, we do not run RL experiments to validate that resulting policy gradient updates are stable and effective at VLA scale. 6 Conclusion Across six flow matching VLAs from 450M to 4.7B parameters, plus a 211 211\, M DiT, four simulation benchmarks and a real world Franka suite, we find the assumption that multi-step inference is necessary for task performance does not hold for well-trained large VLAs. Where multi-step helps, the benefit is localised to smaller models on long-horizon tasks. Our ablations trace step-invariance to a combination of large scale models, training maturity and the quality of the pretrained VLM features rather than to large-scale robot-action pretraining which we find to be not necessary. The key implication is deployment latency: N N multiplies action-head compute at every replanning step, limiting control frequency. A single Euler step removes this overhead with negligible impact on success rate, enabling low-latency deployment of existing flow-matching VLA checkpoints without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives. The same property makes single-backward-pass actor updates attractive for RL post-training without differentiating through the integration chain.
